This is an affliction, not the object of an affliction.

Regarding the phrase "contrary to its nature" (*tad-viparīta*) and so forth, this explains *vijñāna* and *jñāna*.

Because this wisdom (*jñāna*) is contrary to that nature, it is called "contrary to its nature."

as it acts as an obstacle to the wisdom of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* is cited to testify to these two liberations.

Next, the following passage provides a further explanation of the *Dharmadhāraṇī* and *Prajñāvimukti*.
It says in the *Dharmadhāraṇī*:
To have unobstructed knowledge regarding all that is knowable is termed "purity of wisdom. Therefore,
the commentary states:
Because of ignorance, there is obstruction to knowledge;
if ignorance is destroyed, one knows there is no obstruction.
Thus, ignorance is what obstructs the realization of wisdom.
This is called the obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because one destroys ignorance, one attains unobstructed knowledge.
Subsequently, one is led into the Mahāyāna.
This serves to demonstrate that ignorance (*avidyā*) has the meaning of being an obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
However, because the name "ignorance" is common [to both types], it must be distinguished:
only supramundane ignorance is termed an obstruction to knowledge.
"Both obstacles are afflictions" refers to the difficulty of further transformation.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are both afflictions.
For what reason is ignorance alone designated as an affliction that constitutes an obstruction to knowledge?
The following section provides the explanation for this.
Craving is an affliction, and afflictions are distinct from wisdom.
Although ignorance is also called an affliction,
afflictions are themselves wisdom.
Therefore, ignorance is not the same as craving;
this is why they are divided into two distinct obstacles.
Next, an example is cited to explain the obstacle of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The segmentation [of existence] is birth-and-death, and birth-and-death is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If birth-and-death were unconditioned, then birth-and-death would be unconditioned.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is also like this.

It is precisely because it takes its name from its essential nature that it is called "obstruction to knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Therefore, it is said that ignorance (*avidyā*) receives the name "obstruction to knowledge.
As for craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is explained in the section on the four abidings as an affliction (*kleśa*), not an obscuration of knowledge itself.
Therefore, when wisdom is present, there are no afflictions;
when afflictions are present, there is no wisdom.
For this reason, the text says:
Delusion and awakening do not coexist.
Afflictions that constitute an obstruction are called the "affliction-obstruction" (kleśāvaraṇa).
As for what is termed "unconditioned birth-and-death" (asaṃskṛta-saṃsāra):
Among the seven types of birth and death established in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
there is "birth and death through skillful means," which is precisely "unconditioned birth and death";
and there is "birth and death through causes and conditions," which is precisely "birth and death within the dharmadhātu."
These two types of birth and death exist within the land of transformation;
therefore, that birth and death is itself unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus, by way of analogy, it is now understood that delusion is itself wisdom.
Furthermore, craving (tṛṣṇā) is able to cause the continuity of existence to proceed.
To explain further, craving and ignorance (avidyā) differ in their essential natures.
Craving arises from the fruit and is able to continue the subsequent fruit;
therefore, it is said that it can cause the various realms of existence (*bhava*) to continue in succession.
This clarifies the functional capacity of craving.
The phrase "able to cause mental affliction" explains that the function of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is simply that of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The phrase "though obscured by ignorance" sets forth the function of ignorance (*avidyā*; *moha*); when compared with the other afflictions, [ignorance is the most fundamental].
That which attracts the powerful does not exceed craving;
therefore, it receives its name from its power.
For this reason, craving alone is designated as "affliction" (*kleśa*).
It is not called an obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "ignorance (*avidyā*) does not clearly comprehend" below:
this correctly explains that the function of ignorance constitutes the meaning of an obstruction to knowledge.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) both oppose liberation;
yet, while ignorance and craving differ in their status as root and branch,
it is ignorance that serves as the root and directly opposes liberation.
Transgression is itself an obstruction.
Next, from the phrase "the nature of craving" (*tṛṣṇā-svabhāva*) downward, it clarifies that craving is a branch.
Since the root has already been given the name "obstruction to knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), [craving is now identified as its branch].
Therefore, craving is designated merely as an affliction (*kleśa*).
Next, regarding the statement "the nature of ignorance is delusion," this is a further explanation that ignorance is the primary factor capable of obstructing wisdom.
The essential nature is further deluded;
this delusion is itself an obscuration,
for it directly obstructs wisdom.
Therefore, it is called "the meaning of obscuring wisdom is revealed.
Next, regarding the two kinds of ignorance (*avidyā*) below,
this further distinguishes that while the names are the same, their entities are different.
Having distinguished that the essential natures and characteristics of the two obstacles are different,
he first asks: "Although there is a distinction between delusion regarding phenomena and delusion regarding principle..."
Since both are equally designated as "ignorance" (avidyā),
why is ignorance specifically termed an "obstruction to knowledge" (jñeyāvaraṇa)?
Next, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* is cited to answer this.
If discussed generally,
since that which is obstructed is equally termed "wisdom," that which acts as the obstruction is likewise equally termed an "obstruction."
Now, regarding those who argue separately:
since the nature of the wisdom that is obstructed differs,
the ignorance that acts as the obstructor must likewise differ.
Therefore, for those of the two vehicles, the wisdom of selflessness is that which is obstructed,
and it is precisely the afflictions that serve as the obstructor.
The wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmyajñāna) of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is that which is obstructed,
while the wisdom of the selflessness of persons (pudgalanairātmyajñāna) is that which acts as the obstruction.
That which constitutes an obstruction for those of the two vehicles is what serves as an ability to obstruct for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
thus, it is termed "wisdom" with respect to persons of the two vehicles.
Regarding the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, these are merely termed "obstructions.
Since this is also wisdom that constitutes an obstruction, it is called the "obstruction to wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
If this is so, then [the text] below judges it as being held by those directed toward the stages (*bhūmi*).
The selflessness of persons and phenomena are both objects of delusion.
Both the selflessness of persons and phenomena are termed "principle.
The wisdom that realizes both forms of selflessness is termed "pure wisdom."
Both afflictions and knowledge are obstacles for those who possess wisdom and principle.
From the phrase "furthermore, that which is known by wisdom" onward, it means that the knowledge of phenomena is obstructed; thus, it constitutes the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Next, the passage beginning with "If that were so" interrogates the preceding explanation:
if both delusion regarding phenomena (*vastu*) and delusion regarding principles (*tattva*) are termed cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
what is definitively established as such?
Proceeding from the perspectives of illuminating phenomena and illuminating principle,
it is reasonable to understand that both interpretations are valid,
as there are two different explanations provided by the ancients.
Alternatively, being obstructed by various phenomena is called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);
or, ignorance obstructs the Buddha-wisdom.
This is called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Since the Master of the Treatise [Vasubandhu] accepts both [positions], it is said that "although there are two, the two are non-dual. Why is this so?
It is simply that a single wisdom can illumine both phenomena and principle;
although phenomena and principle differ, the essence of wisdom is without distinction.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover, the mind and wisdom become obstacles" presents an alternative interpretation.
Some say that when mind and intellect constitute an obstruction,
"mind" refers to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Discrimination constitutes the objective entity;
the obstruction of the entity is as it truly is.
This explanation takes those who are deluded regarding principle as the subject.
This is called the obstruction of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It is eliminated by the cessation of perception and the cessation of mind.
Here, the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) is cited to provide an explanation in contrast to the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).
For example, when followers of the Hīnayāna enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), where perception ceases and the mind ceases,
this is also called the "knowledge of cessation" (*nirodhajñāna*);
yet this is merely a state of annihilation.
Now, although the mind that obstructs wisdom is extinguished, it cannot be extinguished [in its essence].
Thus, one abandons conceptualization and enters into non-conceptualization;
therefore, know that conceptualization is in truth not something that can be abandoned.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the wisdom of the Middle Way are explained separately in successive layers;
they are not distinct categories.
The cognitive obscuration is ignorance (*avidyā*), and ignorance is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, the cognitive hindrance cannot be severed.
Next, the following passage from a sutra is cited as proof:
"Even merit does not approach the ultimate by even a hair's breadth."
One should know that the essence of discriminating wisdom has no abandonment;
for the sake of aiding the path, it first destroys the afflictions. Once the afflictions are destroyed, [the path is fulfilled].
This wisdom that destroys delusions is,
in its essence, realized wisdom;
therefore, there is no fault.
People create a one-sided distinction between those who sever [delusions] and those who do not; however, when examining the essence of wisdom,
that essence is fundamentally without differentiation.
The various explanations above clarify that although ignorance is called an "obstruction to wisdom," the essence of the obstruction is itself wisdom.
Furthermore, the various interpretations presented previously do not go beyond the meaning of the initial explanation regarding how wisdom is an obstruction when first arising.
The opening provides three explanations.
The first states that "wisdom is explained as an obstruction," which means that wisdom itself functions as the obstructing agent.
The two characters "wisdom-obstruction" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) both belong to the category of the agent.
As for the subsequent statement, "it is called wisdom-obstruction because it arises from that which is obstructed," [this refers to the object].
That is to say, when realized wisdom (pratyakṣajñāna) is obstructed, it is termed the "obstruction to knowledge" (jñeyāvaraṇa).
Both characters of the term "obstruction to knowledge" pertain to that which is obstructed.
Next, regarding the statement, "Furthermore, that which obstructs what is known by wisdom is called the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa)": here,

The subsequent question and answer serve to further clarify potential objections.
The intent of the initial question concerns the sequence of stages from beginning to end as set forth in the *Ratnavali-sutra* (瓔珞經).

One must not dogmatically insist that the distinct stage of the *yǐngluò* (necklace) is fixed exclusively to the first bhūmi.
To clarify the stages in full detail, nothing exceeds the *yǐngluò*;
